--- title: "Distributional assumptions" description: "Most machine-learning models predict without Normal data or equal spread, but the loss still decides what a prediction means. A random forest's errors fail both checks and it predicts well anyway; trained on log counts, it predicts far fewer animals than were caught." order: 2 categories: [assumptions] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Normal data and equal spread are not requirements of machine learning Statistics courses teach two checks before a model is fitted: that the model's errors follow a [Normal distribution](../01-introduction/discriminative-and-generative-models.qmd) (the bell curve), and that their spread is the same everywhere, **equal spread** (homogeneity of variance, in statistics). Counts of animals usually fail both: they are **skewed**, with a long tail of large catches on one side. Most machine-learning models predict without either assumption: trees, forests and boosting split the data by the order of its values, whatever its shape. The exception is a [generative model](../01-introduction/discriminative-and-generative-models.qmd), which describes the data with a shape. The distribution still matters to what a prediction means, and the loss decides it. This page fits one random forest to the survey's counts, checks its errors against both assumptions, and shows how a common fix for skewed data quietly changes what the forest predicts. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Each loss aims at a different middle of the data A prediction is one number standing for all the catches a station could give, and the loss decides which number. [Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd) set squared error against absolute error. Squared error is smallest at the average of the catches, and absolute error at the median, the middle catch. A **quantile loss** aims at any chosen point: its 95% version at the catch that only 1 in 20 stations exceed. For a symmetric bell curve the average and the median are the same. For skewed counts they are not: a few large catches pull the average above the typical one. A model fitted with squared error predicts the average, which is what a total needs: predicted animals per station times the number of stations. Any step that changes what the loss aims at changes that total, and the worked example shows a common one. ::: {.diagram} ![The errors of a model fitted to counts are skewed and spread wider where more is predicted. Each loss aims at a different point of the catches: absolute error at the median, squared error at the average, a quantile loss at any chosen point. Squared error on log counts aims near the median, below the average, so totals come out short.](img/spread.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Skewed errors, widen as predictions grow: a scatter of points that fans out to the right around a rising line; most models predict well anyway, and the checks say where to take care. Each loss aims at a different point: a histogram of catches with a long right tail, a dashed line at the median, a solid line further right at the average and a dotted line far out at the 95% point; absolute error aims at the median, squared error at the average, a quantile loss at any chosen point. Totals, log counts fall short: three bars, the total caught, the total from a model on raw counts level with it, and a clearly shorter total from a model on log counts, marked short. A note says that for skewed counts the loss decides which middle a prediction stands for."} ::: ## Worked example The data, the split by site and the recipe are those of [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd), with missing values filled with the median. The training sites are dealt into ten folds for cross-validation by site, as in [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) |> mutate(log_abundance = log(abundance + 1)) # ten folds of training sites folds <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = site_id, v = 10) tree_recipe <- recipe( abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = train ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) tibble(stations = nrow(train), empty = sum(train$abundance == 0), median = median(train$abundance), average = round(mean(train$abundance), 1), largest = max(train$abundance)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| empty| median| average| largest| |--------:|-----:|------:|-------:|-------:| | 598| 129| 3| 4| 40|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, GroupShuffleSplit, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows] # ten folds of training sites folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=123) # scikit-learn's trees need numbers, so the recipe also makes 0/1 columns. tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) def pipeline(model): return Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", model)]) counts = train["abundance"] pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(train)], "empty": [(counts == 0).sum()], "median": [counts.median()], "average": [round(counts.mean(), 1)], "largest": [counts.max()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | empty | median | average | largest | |-----------:|--------:|---------:|----------:|----------:| | 575 | 133 | 2 | 3.7 | 37 | ::: ::: ::: The counts are far from a bell curve. 129 of the 598 training stations caught nothing, the median station caught 3 animals and the largest 40, and the long tail lifts the average to 4.0. ### The forest's errors are skewed and widen with its predictions A model's errors are the place to check both assumptions, and they must be errors on sites the model did not see. Cross-validation gives one for every training station: each fold's stations are predicted by a forest fitted to the other nine folds. The forest is that of [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd), here with 500 trees, fitted with squared error. The errors are then split into fifths by the size of the prediction. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} forest_model <- rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) forest <- workflow(tree_recipe, forest_model) # every training station, predicted by a forest that never saw its site errors <- fit_resamples(forest, folds, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> transmute(caught = abundance, predicted = .pred, error = caught - predicted, fifth = ntile(predicted, 5)) spread <- errors |> summarise(predicted_from = min(predicted), predicted_to = max(predicted), error_sd = sd(error), .by = fifth) |> arrange(fifth) spread |> mutate(across(-fifth, \(x) round(x, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| fifth| predicted_from| predicted_to| error_sd| |-----:|--------------:|------------:|--------:| | 1| 0.2| 2.1| 1.8| | 2| 2.1| 3.4| 3.1| | 3| 3.4| 4.5| 4.6| | 4| 4.5| 5.9| 4.2| | 5| 5.9| 23.8| 7.7|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} forest = pipeline(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123)) # every training station, predicted by a forest that never saw its site predicted = cross_val_predict(forest, train[predictors], counts, groups=train["site_id"], cv=folds) errors = pd.DataFrame({"caught": counts.to_numpy(), "predicted": predicted}) errors["error"] = errors["caught"] - errors["predicted"] errors["fifth"] = pd.qcut(errors["predicted"].rank(method="first"), 5, labels=False) + 1 spread = (errors.groupby("fifth") .agg(predicted_from=("predicted", "min"), predicted_to=("predicted", "max"), error_sd=("error", "std")) .reset_index()) spread.round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | fifth | predicted_from | predicted_to | error_sd | |--------:|-----------------:|---------------:|-----------:| | 1 | 0.4 | 2.1 | 1.9 | | 2 | 2.1 | 3.1 | 3.2 | | 3 | 3.1 | 4 | 4.9 | | 4 | 4 | 5.2 | 3.9 | | 5 | 5.2 | 12.4 | 5.5 | ::: ::: ::: @fig-errors shows both checks. The errors are not Normal: 62% of the stations caught fewer animals than predicted, the middle station 0.9 fewer, while a few caught far more, up to 30 above the prediction. The spread is not equal either. In the fifth of stations with the smallest predictions the errors have a standard deviation of 1.8 animals, and in the fifth with the largest, 7.7: 4.3 times as wide. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} middle_90 <- errors |> summarise(from = min(predicted), to = max(predicted), low = quantile(error, 0.05), high = quantile(error, 0.95), .by = fifth) shape_plot <- ggplot(errors, aes(error)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.7) + geom_function(fun = \(x) nrow(errors) * dnorm(x, mean(errors$error), sd(errors$error)), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "Error, caught − predicted (individuals)", y = "Stations", title = "Skewed, not bell-shaped") spread_plot <- ggplot(errors, aes(predicted, error)) + geom_rect(data = middle_90, aes(xmin = from, xmax = to, ymin = low, ymax = high), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], alpha = 0.15) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") + geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.2) + labs(x = "Predicted count", y = "Error (individuals)", title = "Wider where more is predicted") shape_plot + spread_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The random forest's errors on sites it did not see, one for each training station. Left: their histogram, against a Normal curve with the same mean and spread; the errors bunch below zero and trail far above it. Right: each error against the prediction, with the middle 90% of the errors in each fifth of the predictions shaded; the errors spread wider as the prediction grows.](distributional-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-errors-1.png){#fig-errors fig-alt='Two panels. Left, a histogram of the errors in individuals, with a Normal curve of the same mean and standard deviation drawn over it: the histogram peaks just below zero, where 62% of the errors lie, and has a long tail to the right reaching 30, which the symmetric Normal curve does not follow. Right, the errors against the predicted count, with five shaded boxes, one for each fifth of the predictions, covering the middle 90% of the errors: the box for the smallest predictions is narrow and the boxes grow taller to the right, where the standard deviation reaches 7.7 animals against 1.8 on the left.' width=1700} ::: ::: ::: Neither stops the forest. Its predictions are averages of the catches at similar stations, and an average needs no particular shape and no equal spread. The shape matters to how sure a prediction can be: an interval around it should be lopsided and widen where the errors do, which [Communicating uncertainty](../10-interpretation/communicating-uncertainty.qmd) builds. It also matters to what a prediction means, the subject of the next part. ### Training on log counts predicts far fewer animals than were caught A common recipe for skewed data is to make it more Normal first: fit the model to the log of the count, plus 1 so that empty stations stay at zero, and turn each prediction back with the exponential, minus 1. The second forest does exactly that, and both are scored on the same cross-validated stations: by RMSE, and by the total number of animals they predict across the 598 stations against the total caught. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} log_recipe <- recipe( log_abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = train ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) log_predicted <- fit_resamples(workflow(log_recipe, forest_model), folds, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> pull(.pred) errors <- errors |> mutate(log_predicted = exp(log_predicted) - 1) # back to animals totals <- tibble( model = c("Random forest", "Random forest on log counts"), rmse = c(rmse_vec(errors$caught, errors$predicted), rmse_vec(errors$caught, errors$log_predicted)), predicted_total = c(sum(errors$predicted), sum(errors$log_predicted)), caught_total = sum(errors$caught) ) totals |> mutate(rmse = round(rmse, 2), predicted_total = round(predicted_total)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | rmse| predicted_total| caught_total| |:---------------------------|----:|---------------:|------------:| |Random forest | 4.69| 2514| 2421| |Random forest on log counts | 4.78| 1699| 2421|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} log_predicted = cross_val_predict(forest, train[predictors], np.log(counts + 1), groups=train["site_id"], cv=folds) errors["log_predicted"] = np.exp(log_predicted) - 1 # back to animals totals = pd.DataFrame({ "model": ["Random forest", "Random forest on log counts"], "rmse": [root_mean_squared_error(errors["caught"], errors[column]) for column in ["predicted", "log_predicted"]], "predicted_total": [errors["predicted"].sum(), errors["log_predicted"].sum()], "caught_total": errors["caught"].sum(), }) totals.round({"rmse": 2, "predicted_total": 0}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | rmse | predicted_total | caught_total | |:----------------------------|-------:|------------------:|---------------:| | Random forest | 4.11 | 2142 | 2128 | | Random forest on log counts | 4.27 | 1445 | 2128 | ::: ::: ::: The two forests score almost the same: an RMSE of 4.69 on raw counts and 4.78 on log counts. Their totals do not. The stations caught 2421 animals; the forest on raw counts predicts 2514, and the forest on log counts 1699, 30% short. @fig-log shows that the shortfall runs through every fifth of the stations, not just the largest. On the log scale, squared error aims at the average log count. Turned back into animals, that is close to the median, the typical catch, and for skewed counts the typical catch sits below the average. The forest on log counts answers a different question, and the RMSE does not show it. A survey that sums its predictions into a stock estimate, a biomass or a map total would come out 30% short with no warning. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} by_fifth |> pivot_longer(-fifth, names_to = "series", values_to = "animals") |> mutate(series = fct_inorder(series)) |> ggplot(aes(fifth, animals, colour = series)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.5) + scale_colour_manual(values = c( "Caught" = "grey40", "Random forest" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Random forest on log counts" = ml_palette[["vermilion"]])) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) + labs(x = "Fifth of the stations, by the forest's prediction", y = "Average count (individuals)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The average catch per station in each fifth of the forest's predictions, against the average each forest predicts there. The forest on raw counts follows the catch; the forest on log counts falls short in every fifth.](distributional-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-log-1.png){#fig-log fig-alt='Points joined by lines for five groups of training stations, ordered by the forest prediction, with the average count per station on the vertical axis. The caught averages, in grey, rise from 1.4 to 7.2. The forest on raw counts, in blue, lies close to them. The forest on log counts, in vermilion, lies below them in every group, from 0.8 to 5.5.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: Keep the counts as they are when the totals matter. For a skewed outcome, a loss built for it, such as the Poisson deviance of [Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd), changes the weights without changing what the prediction aims at. Every check on this page also treats the stations as independent, which [Dependent data](dependent-data.qmd) tests. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Most machine-learning models predict without Normal data or **equal spread**. For **skewed** counts, the loss still decides what a prediction means. - Squared error aims at the average, absolute error at the median, and a **quantile loss** at any chosen point. For skewed counts these differ. - The random forest's errors on unseen sites were skewed, and 4.3 times as spread out at the largest predictions as at the smallest. Its predictions did not need either assumption. - Trained on log counts, the forest scored about the same RMSE but predicted 30% fewer animals than were caught: it aimed at the typical catch, not the average. Keep the counts as they are when totals matter. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Replace the forest with linear regression, `linear_reg()`, and fit it to the raw counts and to the log counts. Is the shortfall in the total larger or smaller than the forest's? 2. Fit the boosted model of [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) to the raw counts with Poisson deviance, `set_engine("xgboost", objective = "count:poisson")`, and compare its total with the forest's.
